claims.text: A computational method combining disorder-refined interatomic potentials with anharmonic lattice dynamics will predict low phonon thermal conductivity in high-entropy alloys more accurately than current models.
High-entropy alloys with significant configurational disorder typically contain five or more principal elements.
The proposed approach can encode configurational disorder through explicit disorder parameters in refined interatomic potentials.
Anharmonic lattice-dynamics calculations can directly calculate phonon scattering and phonon lifetimes in the targeted alloys.
Phonon scattering dominates heat transport in the targeted high-entropy alloys from ambient to moderately elevated temperatures.
Configurational disorder in the alloy lattice enhances phonon scattering.
Enhanced phonon scattering caused by configurational disorder reduces phonon lifetimes.
Reduced phonon lifetimes lead to lower phonon thermal conductivity.
Explicit disorder modeling will incorporate disorder-induced increases in phonon scattering rates.
Combining disorder-refined potentials with anharmonicity will produce more realistic phonon-lifetime calculations.
Phonon lifetime is a key determinant of low phonon thermal conductivity.
The proposed approach will reduce phonon-thermal-conductivity prediction error by at least 20–30% relative to current empirical or simplified first-principles models.
Existing empirical correlations and first-principles simulations often underestimate the effect of compositional disorder on phonon scattering in high-entropy systems.
The approach is expected to be applicable only to alloys with sufficiently high configurational disorder, characterized here as typically five or more principal elements.
The approach is not expected to apply when alternate heat-transfer mechanisms, such as electron–phonon interactions in metallic regimes, dominate.
Quantitative calibration of the proposed disorder parameters remains uncertain.
The operational temperature range over which anharmonic lattice dynamics adequately captures phonon scattering remains uncertain.
The method requires validation over a broader high-entropy-alloy compositional space.
Time-domain thermoreflectance or a similar technique can be used to measure phonon thermal conductivity over the relevant temperature range.
Failure to achieve the stated 20–30% prediction-error reduction, or failure to reproduce the predicted conductivity decrease with increasing disorder, would falsify the hypothesis.
